title: Permanent Establishment Checker | Which Province Wants a Return
content:
Provincial

Permanent Establishment Checker

A permanent establishment is a fixed place through which a corporation carries on business. Quebec and Alberta collect their own corporate income tax.

Three answersQuebec and AlbertaCO-17 and AT1 separateFederal T2 either way

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

Last reviewed: November 9, 2026

Where the corporation has a fixed place of business

Answer the three questions above.

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

What a Permanent Establishment Is

A fixed place through which the corporation carries on business. For a dormant corporation that is generally its registered office, which is why a company that does nothing all year still has an establishment somewhere.

It matters because two provinces collect their own corporate income tax. An establishment in either one brings that province’s return with it, in addition to the federal T2, and the guide to the Quebec CO-17 and the Alberta AT1 sets out both.

Which Provinces Collect Their Own

Where the establishment isThe provincial returnIs it separate from the T2
QuebecCO-17Yes, a separate return
AlbertaAT1Yes, a separate return
OntarioCollected with the federal returnNo separate provincial income tax return
Anywhere elseNot named on this siteThis site states no other provincial return

The last row is deliberate. This site publishes the Quebec and Alberta position because those two administer their own corporate income tax, and it does not state a position for provinces it has not published.

What That Means for the Fee

A corporation with a Quebec or Alberta permanent establishment needs work this service does not price, and pretending otherwise would be worse than saying so.

So this page is a boundary rather than a quotation. Where the answers bring a CO-17 or an AT1 into play, the work is outside nil T2 filing at $300.00 plus HST per tax year. Where they do not, the federal return is the whole of it. The provincial return requirement checker asks the same question from the other end.

Where the corporation has its fixed place of business is a different question from whether the year was nil, and this page answers only the first.

Frequently Asked Questions

What counts as a permanent establishment?

A fixed place through which the corporation carries on business. For a dormant corporation that is generally its registered office.

My corporation is dormant. Does it have one?

Generally yes, at its registered office. Being dormant does not remove the address, and the address is what the test turns on.

Why only Quebec and Alberta?

Because those two administer their own corporate income tax, so each has its own return. Ontario corporate tax is collected with the federal return instead.

Is the CO-17 part of the T2?

No. Quebec administers its own corporate income tax, so the CO-17 is a separate return filed in addition to the federal one.

Is the AT1 part of the T2?

No. The same applies in Alberta: the AT1 is a separate provincial return.

Do you file the CO-17 or the AT1?

No. A corporation with a Quebec or Alberta permanent establishment needs work this service does not price, and pretending otherwise would be worse than saying so.

I am registered in Quebec but have no office there.

Registration and a fixed place of business are different questions. What this page asks about is the fixed place.

Does an establishment make the year not nil?

Not by itself. Where the corporation has its fixed place of business and whether it did anything in the year are two separate questions.

What if I have establishments in two provinces?

Then each province that collects its own corporate income tax wants its own return. The table above names them one at a time.

What is the federal position either way?

The T2 is owed within six months of the fiscal year-end wherever the establishment is.

title: Carrying On Business Checker | Holding Is Not Doing
content:
Is the Year Nil

Carrying On Business in Canada Checker

Holding a bank account, owning assets and staying registered are not carrying on business, and every one of those years is nil.

Four answersHolding is not doingOne answer decides itA nil year either way

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

Last reviewed: November 9, 2026

What the corporation did, and what it merely had

Answer all four questions above.

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

Having Something and Doing Something

A corporation can hold a bank account, own assets and stay registered for years without carrying on business, and every one of those years is nil. That sentence does most of the work on this page.

The confusion is understandable. A corporation that still owns a building, still has a bank balance and is still on the register looks active from outside. None of those is the corporation carrying on business, and the guide to zero-activity corporate tax returns works through the same distinction at length.

What Decides It, and What Does Not

In the yearCarrying on businessEffect on the nil question
A bank account heldNoThe year can still be nil
Assets ownedNoThe year can still be nil
Registration kept upNoThe year can still be nil
Something sold or invoicedYesThe year is not nil
Someone employedYesThe year is not nil

One caution on the first row. A bank account that pays interest is a different matter: interest credited on a balance is investment income, and the corporation is not nil for that tax year. Holding the account is not activity; being paid on it is income.

What This Page Does Not Answer

It does not tell you whether a return is owed. One is, for every tax year, whether or not the corporation carried on business, and it is due within six months of the fiscal year-end.

Nor does it decide the schedules. What the corporation holds does that, which is the point of the required schedules checker, and nil T2 filing at $300.00 plus HST per tax year covers the return either way.

Holding things is not the same as doing things, and that distinction is the whole of this page.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is holding a bank account carrying on business?

No. A corporation can hold a bank account, own assets and stay registered for years without carrying on business, and every one of those years is nil.

My corporation owns a building and nothing else happened.

Owning an asset is not carrying on business. If rent came in, that is different: a rental corporation is not nil.

The bank paid a few dollars of interest.

Then the year is not nil. Interest credited on a balance is investment income, whatever the amount, even though holding the account is not activity.

I invoiced one client and nothing else.

That is carrying on business, and the year is not nil.

Does a return still have to be filed?

Yes, for every tax year, within six months of the fiscal year-end. This page answers whether the year was nil, not whether a return is owed.

What about a corporation that has never traded at all?

Then nothing was held and nothing done, and the GIFI exemption may actually apply, which it rarely does once there is share capital or a bank balance.

Is paying a bank charge activity?

It is an expense rather than carrying on business, so the year can still be nil, but it is something to report and that makes the GIFI schedules required.

Does keeping the registration up count?

No. Staying on the register is not carrying on business, though the registry still wants its annual return.

Does this decide which schedules I file?

No. What the corporation holds decides those, not what it did.

Is a dormant year covered by the fee?

Yes. Nil T2 filing at $300.00 plus HST per tax year covers a year like that.

title: Non-Resident Corporation Filing Checker | What Is Owed
content:
Non-Resident

Non-Resident Corporation Filing Checker

A corporation incorporated in Canada files a T2 whoever owns it. Non-resident ownership changes what a late return costs.

Three answersOwnership is not residence$25.00 per day if lateA nil year is still filed

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

Last reviewed: November 9, 2026

The corporation and the year

Answer the three questions above.

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

Ownership and Incorporation Are Two Questions

A corporation incorporated in Canada files a T2 for every tax year, within six months of its fiscal year-end, whoever its shareholders are and wherever they live. Non-resident ownership does not remove the return.

What it does change is the cost of being late, and that is the part worth knowing in advance. The guide to non-resident-owned corporation nil filing sets out the position in full.

What a Late Return Costs Here

The corporationA late nil returnWhy
Resident-owned, nil yearNo percentage late-filing penalty on a nil yearThat penalty is a percentage of tax owing, and the corporation owes $0.00
Non-resident-owned, nil year$25.00 per day, to a maximum of $2,500.00It applies regardless, because it does not depend on tax owing
Either, unfiled and leftThe year stays openIt invites a demand to file and an arbitrary assessment, and blocks a clearance certificate

The second row is the one that catches people out. Every other argument for leaving a nil year unfiled rests on there being no tax owing, and this charge does not.

A Corporation Incorporated Outside Canada

That is a different question and this page does not settle it. Whether Canada wants a return from a corporation incorporated elsewhere turns on whether it carries on business in Canada, which the carrying on business in Canada checker and the permanent establishment checker each take from a different side.

What this page answers is the common case: a Canadian corporation whose owners are not in Canada. Nil T2 filing at $300.00 plus HST per tax year covers those years.

Who owns the corporation changes what a late return costs. It does not change whether one is owed.

Frequently Asked Questions

My shareholders live abroad. Do I still file a T2?

Yes. A corporation incorporated in Canada files a T2 for every tax year, whoever owns it and wherever they live.

Does a nil year still have to be filed?

Yes, and for a non-resident-owned corporation that matters more than usual, because a late one is charged $25.00 per day up to $2,500.00.

Why is the penalty different?

Because it does not depend on tax owing. The percentage late-filing penalty is a percentage of tax owing and a nil return owes $0.00; this charge applies regardless.

Is the maximum really $2,500.00?

That is the maximum published for this charge, reached at 100 days.

My corporation was incorporated outside Canada.

Then this page does not settle it. That turns on whether the corporation carries on business in Canada, which is a separate test.

Does non-resident ownership make the year not nil?

No. Who owns the corporation and what it did in the year are separate questions.

Does the six-month deadline change?

No. The return is due within six months of the fiscal year-end either way.

Do you file for non-resident-owned corporations?

A nil year is covered at $300.00 plus HST per tax year, the same as any other nil year.

What if several years are unfiled?

Each year is its own return and the daily charge runs on each late one. They are filed oldest first.

Where is the whole position set out?

In the guide to non-resident-owned corporation nil filing.

title: Outstanding Returns Count | How Many T2 Years Are Open
content:
Unfiled Years

Outstanding Returns Count Checker

One T2 falls due for each tax year, six months after the year-end. This counts the years that have passed their filing date.

One date inCounts the tax sideDates each filing dayOldest first

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

Last reviewed: November 9, 2026

The last return you filed

Enter the year-end of the last return you filed.

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

One Return for Each Tax Year

A corporation files a T2 for every tax year it has existed, due within six months of the fiscal year-end. So the count is mechanical: one return for each year-end that has passed, and the filing date six months after each.

The calculator above walks the year-ends forward from the last return you filed and dates each filing day, so a year that has ended but not yet reached its filing date is shown as not yet due rather than as outstanding.

What the Count Is Not

TrailWhat falls due each yearWhat counts it
The corporate tax returnOne T2, six months after the fiscal year-endThis page
The Ontario annual returnOne registry filing for each tax yearThe Ontario missed annual returns calculator
The federal annual returnOne filing, 60 days after the anniversaryThe federal annual return anniversary calculator

The three are separate trails to three different bodies, and being current on one says nothing about the others. This page counts the first row only.

What Happens to the Years It Counts

An unfiled year does not expire. It stays open, invites a demand to file and an arbitrary assessment, and blocks a clearance certificate until it is filed. That is why the count matters more than it looks.

They are filed oldest first and can be transmitted together, each at $300.00 plus HST per tax year. The unfiled years cost calculator totals them and the guide to catching up on unfiled corporate tax returns sets out the order.

The count is the easy part. Filing them oldest first is the part that closes the years.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many returns am I behind?

One for each tax year-end that has passed its filing date since the last return you filed. The calculator above counts them and dates each one.

What is the filing date?

Six months after the fiscal year-end, moved to the next business day where it falls on a weekend or a holiday.

A year has ended but the six months are not up.

Then it is not outstanding yet, and the table says so rather than counting it.

Do unfiled years expire?

No. An unfiled year stays open, invites a demand to file and an arbitrary assessment, and blocks a clearance certificate until it is filed.

I changed my year-end part way through.

Then the count is indicative only. A changed year-end produces a short tax year, so the year-ends are not a plain run of anniversaries.

Is this the same as the annual returns I owe?

No. Those are registry filings on their own trails. This page counts the corporate tax returns only.

Can they all be filed at once?

They are prepared oldest first and can be transmitted together.

What does each one cost?

A nil year is $300.00 plus HST per tax year, one price for each return.

What if some of those years were not nil?

Then those years are not covered by that fee. A holding corporation with investment income, a rental corporation and a corporation that paid or received a dividend are not nil.

I do not know when the last one was filed.

The corporation’s own records settle it. The count runs from whatever date you enter, so an uncertain date gives an uncertain count.

title: Schedule 11 Shareholder Transactions | Movement or Balance
content:
Schedules

Schedule 11 Shareholder Transactions Checker

Schedule 11 reports transactions with shareholders, officers and employees. A balance that did not move in the year is not a transaction.

Three answersMovement, not balanceA dormant year often has noneBalances go to GIFI

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

Last reviewed: November 9, 2026

Shareholder dealings in the tax year

Answer the three questions above.

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

A Transaction Is Movement, Not a Balance

Schedule 11 reports transactions with shareholders, officers and employees. The word doing the work is transaction: something has to have moved during the year.

That is why most dormant years have nothing for it. A shareholder loan sitting at the same figure it was a year ago is a balance, and a balance is reported where balances are reported. The shareholder loan balance checker deals with the balance itself.

Where Each One Goes

What happenedIs it a transactionWhere it is reported
Money advanced to a shareholder in the yearYesSchedule 11
A shareholder repaid part of a loan in the yearYesSchedule 11
A benefit or payment other than salaryYesSchedule 11
A loan balance unchanged all yearNoThe GIFI schedules, as a balance
Salary paid through payrollNot for this purposePayroll, with its own filings

The fourth row is the one that matters on a nil return, and it is also the row that still has a consequence: a shareholder loan is one of the five things that make GIFI Schedules 100, 125 and 141 required, whichever direction the balance runs.

What a Nil Year Usually Has Here

Nothing, and that is the useful answer. A corporation that did not trade generally did not advance anything to its shareholder or take anything back, so there is no transaction to report even where a loan has sat on the books for years.

Which schedules a nil return does carry is a different list, and the guide to T2 schedules on a nil return gives it: the GIFI schedules where there is anything to report, Schedule 50 for a shareholder at 10% or more, Schedule 24 on a first return, and Schedule 8 with loss continuity. Nil T2 filing at $300.00 plus HST per tax year covers them.

A balance that sat still all year is not a transaction, and that is why most dormant years have nothing for this schedule to report.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Schedule 11 report?

Transactions with shareholders, officers and employees. Something has to have moved during the year for it to have anything to take.

My shareholder loan has not changed in years. Does it go here?

No. A balance that did not move is not a transaction. It is reported where balances are reported, on the GIFI schedules.

I took money out of the corporation this year.

That is a transaction with a shareholder, and it is what this schedule reports.

I repaid part of my shareholder loan.

That is also a transaction. Movement in either direction counts.

Does a dormant corporation file Schedule 11?

Usually there is nothing for it to report, because nothing moved. This page asks the question rather than assuming the answer.

Is salary a transaction for this purpose?

Salary runs through payroll and carries its own filings. What this page asks about is the other dealings.

Does the loan balance matter at all then?

Yes, elsewhere. A shareholder loan is one of the five things that make GIFI Schedules 100, 125 and 141 required, whichever direction it runs.

Is this the same as Schedule 50?

No. Schedule 50 lists shareholders at 10% or more. This one is about dealings with them during the year.

Does a transaction make the year not nil?

Not by itself, and this page does not say it does. Whether the year was nil turns on whether the corporation carried on business or had income.

Which schedules does a nil return actually carry?

The GIFI schedules where there is anything to report, Schedule 50 for a shareholder at 10% or more, Schedule 24 on a first return, and Schedule 8 with loss continuity.
